query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using in-situ atom probe tomography (APT) during controlled high‐temperature oxidation of an additively manufactured dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA will reveal that selective elemental redistribution from Ti- and Cr-rich nanoprecipitates promotes the formation of a protective oxide layer that mitigates further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy with nanoprecipitates dispersed in a homogeneous matrix.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to high-temperature oxidation conditions while performing in-situ APT to track elemental redistribution in real time.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation (representative of gas turbine, power plant, or aerospace operational temperatures) in an oxidizing atmosphere under controlled laboratory settings.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoprecipitates enriched in Ti and Cr that act as local elemental reservoirs.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidation conditions, Ti and Cr preferentially segregate from nanoprecipitates to the alloy/oxide interface, nucleating a dense, protective oxide layer that slows further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: APT measurements will show measurable elemental gradients at nanoprecipitate interfaces with accumulation of Ti and Cr coinciding with early-stage protective oxide formation. This phenomenon would correlate with improved oxidation resistance compared to cast and wrought counterparts.
generation.baseline: The oxidation behavior and elemental distributions observed in cast and wrought forms of the same alloy composition.
generation.boundary: The identified mechanism is expected to dominate under the tested high-temperature oxidizing conditions; variations in oxidation atmosphere or alloy processing parameters may yield different elemental redistribution behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: While APT is well suited to capture atomic-scale redistribution, linking the extent of elemental segregation quantitatively to oxidation retardation requires further confirmation; kinetic factors and transient oxidation phenomena could introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA using additive manufacturing. Expose these samples to a high-temperature oxidizing environment while continuously monitoring the nanoscale elemental distribution using in-situ atom probe tomography. In parallel, prepare control samples via conventional cast/wrought methods under the same oxidation conditions. Compare the degree of elemental segregation at nanoprecipitate interfaces and correlate with oxide layer morphology using complementary TEM/EELS analyses.
measurements: 3D elemental mapping at atomic resolution via APT
Oxide layer characterization (thickness, composition) via TEM/EELS
Mechanical strength and oxidation degradation assessments pre- and post-oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If APT does not reveal significant Ti and Cr segregation at nanoprecipitate interfaces during oxidation, or if there is no observable correlation between elemental redistribution and the formation of a protective oxide layer (as confirmed by TEM/EELS and mechanical tests), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEA, also called multi‐principal‐element refractory alloys) comprise five or more principal elements from the refractory transition metals (group 4–6 elements: Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Mo, and W, often with Ti and Cr also considered), [ [1] , [2] , [3] ] with structural applications under extreme temperature conditions, beyond those where nickel‐based superalloys can be used. [ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD.
